choices.text: It is achiral but can be converted into a chiral molecule in a single chemical step
It is chiral but can be converted into an achiral molecule in a single step
choices.why: That is the reverse. A prochiral molecule starts achiral; one step makes it chiral.

choices.text: It already contains a chirality center that hasn't been assigned R or S yet
choices.why: A molecule with a chirality center is already chiral. Prochirality describes an achiral molecule that is one step away from being chiral.

choices.text: It is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers
choices.why: A racemic mixture contains chiral molecules. A prochiral molecule is itself achiral.

explanation: A molecule is said to be prochiral if it can be converted from achiral to chiral in a single chemical step. For example, 2-butanone is prochiral because adding hydrogen converts it to the chiral alcohol 2-butanol.

prompt: Which ketone is prochiral, giving a chiral alcohol when hydrogen is added to its carbonyl group?

choices.text: 2-Pentanone, CH3COCH2CH2CH3
Acetone, CH3COCH3
choices.why: Adding hydrogen gives 2-propanol, whose C2 carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not a chirality center.

choices.text: 3-Pentanone, CH3CH2COCH2CH3
choices.why: This ketone is symmetrical. Adding hydrogen gives 3-pentanol, whose C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so the product is achiral.

choices.text: Cyclohexanone
choices.why: Adding hydrogen gives cyclohexanol, whose C1 is attached to two identical ring paths, so the product is achiral.

explanation: An unsymmetrical ketone like 2-butanone is prochiral because adding hydrogen converts it to a chiral alcohol. 2-Pentanone is unsymmetrical in the same way: its product, 2-pentanol, has a C2 bearing four different groups (H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH2CH3).

prompt: You look at one face of a trigonal, sp2-hybridized carbon. Its three groups, from highest to third-highest rank, run clockwise. Which face are you looking at?

choices.text: The Re face
The Si face
choices.why: Si is the face on which the arrows from highest to third-highest curve counterclockwise.

choices.text: The R face
choices.why: R and S describe tetrahedral chirality centers. Faces of a planar carbon are named Re and Si (Re is similar to R).

choices.text: It can't be named until the fourth group adds
choices.why: The faces are named from the three groups already on the planar carbon; no fourth group is needed.

explanation: To name a face, rank the three groups on the trigonal carbon and imagine curved arrows from the highest to the second-highest to the third-highest. The face on which the arrows curve clockwise is the Re face (similar to R); the face on which they curve counterclockwise is the Si face (similar to S).

prompt: Viewed from the top, the three groups on a planar carbonyl carbon run counterclockwise in priority order. What is the bottom face?

choices.text: The Re face, because from the bottom the same order runs clockwise
The Si face, the same as the top
choices.why: Turning the molecule over reverses the direction of the arrows, so the two faces always have opposite names.

choices.text: Neither; only the top face of a carbonyl group is named
choices.why: A planar carbon has two faces, and each is named: one Re and one Si.

choices.text: It depends on which face hydrogen actually adds to
choices.why: The names come from the groups on the carbon, not from the reaction. Which face reacts decides which product forms.

explanation: The top face, where the arrows from highest to second-highest to third-highest curve counterclockwise, is the Si face. Seen from the other side, the same arrows curve clockwise, so the bottom face is the Re face. In the figure for 2-butanone, the Re face is at the top and the Si face at the bottom.

prompt: To name the faces of the carbonyl carbon in 2-butanone, CH3COCH2CH3, how are its three groups ranked?

choices.text: O > CH2CH3 > CH3
CH2CH3 > CH3 > O
choices.why: Oxygen has a higher atomic number than carbon, so the carbonyl oxygen ranks first.

choices.text: O > CH3 > CH2CH3
choices.why: Both groups attach through carbon, so look at the next atoms: CH2CH3 has (C, H, H) and CH3 has (H, H, H), so ethyl ranks higher.

choices.text: O > CH2CH3 = CH3, so the faces can't be named
choices.why: The tie at the first atom is broken at the next atoms out, where ethyl wins. If the two carbon groups were truly identical, the ketone wouldn't be prochiral.

explanation: Naming a face means ranking the three groups attached to the trigonal carbon with the sequence rules: oxygen first, then ethyl, then methyl. Arrows O → CH2CH3 → CH3 curve clockwise on the Re face and counterclockwise on the Si face.

prompt: Hydrogen adds to the carbonyl carbon of 2-butanone from its Re face. Which product forms?

choices.text: (S)-2-Butanol
(R)-2-Butanol
choices.why: Re doesn't mean the product will be R. Addition from the Si face gives (R)-2-butanol.

choices.text: A racemic mixture of (R)- and (S)-2-butanol
choices.why: A racemic mixture would form if hydrogen added equally to both faces. Addition from one face gives one enantiomer.

choices.text: 2-Butanone again, because addition from the Re face gives an achiral product
choices.why: 2-Butanol is chiral whichever face hydrogen adds to; the face only decides which enantiomer forms.

explanation: Which enantiomer of 2-butanol is produced depends on which face of the planar carbonyl group undergoes reaction. Addition of hydrogen from the Re face gives (S)-2-butanol, and addition from the Si face gives (R)-2-butanol.

prompt: Which statement about the Re and Si faces is true?

choices.text: Adding a group to the Re face doesn't necessarily give an R product; Re-face addition of hydrogen to 2-butanone gives the S alcohol
Adding a group to the Re face always gives an R chirality center
choices.why: Re is named by analogy with R (clockwise), but the product's configuration must be assigned on its own. For 2-butanone, the Re face gives (S)-2-butanol.

choices.text: Adding a group to the Re face always gives an S chirality center
choices.why: The 2-butanone case is not a general rule; the outcome depends on where the new group ranks among the four groups of the product.

choices.text: Re and Si faces exist only on chiral molecules
choices.why: The faces belong to planar carbons in prochiral molecules such as 2-butanone, which is achiral.

explanation: The Re face is the one on which the arrows from highest to third-highest curve clockwise (similar to R), but the product's R or S label is assigned afresh with the new group in place. In 2-butanone, addition of hydrogen from the Re face gives (S)-2-butanol.

prompt: The carbonyl carbon of acetophenone, C6H5COCH3, has groups ranked O > C6H5 > CH3. Hydrogen adds from the Si face. What is the configuration of the 1-phenylethanol formed?

choices.text: R
S
choices.why: Si does not mean S. From the Si face, O → C6H5 → CH3 runs counterclockwise with the new H pointing toward you; viewed with H away, the order is clockwise, so the center is R.

choices.text: Neither; the product is achiral
choices.why: 1-Phenylethanol has four different groups on the former carbonyl carbon (OH, C6H5, CH3 and H), so it is chiral.

choices.text: It can't be decided without knowing the reaction conditions
choices.why: Once the face is known, the configuration follows from the geometry; that is why the Re/Si labels are useful.

explanation: From the Si face, O → C6H5 → CH3 curves counterclockwise. Hydrogen adds from that side, so in the product the lowest-ranked H points toward the viewer, and OH > C6H5 > CH3 still runs counterclockwise. Viewed from the opposite side, with H away, the order is clockwise: R. This is the same pattern as 2-butanone, where Si-face addition gives (R)-2-butanol.

prompt: Which carbon of chloroethane, CH3CH2Cl, is a prochirality center?

choices.text: The CH2Cl carbon
The CH3 carbon
choices.why: Changing one of its three hydrogens still leaves two identical hydrogens on that carbon, so it doesn't become a chirality center.

choices.text: Both carbons
choices.why: Only the CH2Cl carbon becomes a chirality center when one hydrogen is changed. The CH3 carbon would still carry two hydrogens.

choices.text: Neither carbon, because chloroethane is achiral
choices.why: A prochirality center is found in an achiral molecule; it becomes a chirality center only after one attached group is changed.

explanation: An sp3-hybridized atom is a prochirality center if changing one of its attached groups makes it a chirality center. The CH2Cl carbon carries H, H, Cl and CH3; changing one H gives four different groups, just as with the −CH2OH carbon of ethanol.

prompt: In which compound is the carbon atom a prochirality center?

choices.text: CH2BrCl
CH2Cl2
choices.why: Changing one hydrogen gives CHXCl2, which still has two identical Cl atoms, so the carbon doesn't become a chirality center.

choices.text: CHBrClF
choices.why: This carbon already has four different groups. It is a chirality center, not a prochirality center.

choices.text: CH4
choices.why: Changing one hydrogen of methane still leaves three identical hydrogens.

explanation: A prochirality center becomes a chirality center when one of its attached groups is changed. In CH2BrCl, replacing one H (for example by deuterium) gives CHDBrCl, which has four different groups.

prompt: To label the two hydrogens on the −CH2OH carbon of ethanol, we imagine replacing one ¹H with ²H (deuterium). Why deuterium?

choices.text: It ranks higher than the remaining ¹H but still lower than the other groups on the carbon
It ranks higher than every other group, so it becomes priority 1
choices.why: Deuterium has atomic number 1 like protium; it outranks ¹H only by mass, so it stays below OH and CH3.

choices.text: Deuterium reacts differently from ¹H, so it shows which hydrogen a reaction removes
choices.why: For naming, the replacement is only imagined, to rank one hydrogen over the other. Nothing about reactivity is involved.

choices.text: It makes the carbon a chirality center without changing the rank of anything
choices.why: The point is that the change does raise one hydrogen's rank, over the other hydrogen only, while keeping its rank with respect to the other groups.

explanation: To distinguish two identical atoms on a prochirality center, we imagine a change that raises the ranking of one atom over the other without affecting its rank with respect to other attached groups. The newly introduced ²H ranks higher than the remaining ¹H, but it remains lower than other groups attached to the carbon.

prompt: Why wouldn't imagining one hydrogen of ethanol's −CH2OH carbon replaced by Cl be a good way to decide whether it is pro-R or pro-S?

choices.text: Cl would outrank OH and CH3, changing its rank with respect to the other groups
Cl would not make the carbon a chirality center
choices.why: It would: the carbon would carry Cl, OH, CH3 and H. The problem is that Cl jumps to first priority.

choices.text: Cl ranks lower than hydrogen
choices.why: Chlorine (atomic number 17) ranks far above hydrogen, and above O and C too; that is exactly the problem.

choices.text: Nothing; any replacement atom gives the same pro-R/pro-S labels
choices.why: A replacement that changes the order of the other groups can reverse the R/S result, so the method specifies a change that raises the atom only above its twin.

explanation: The imagined change must raise the ranking of one atom over the other without affecting its rank with respect to other attached groups. Replacing ¹H with ²H does this: deuterium ranks above the remaining ¹H but stays below OH and CH3. Chlorine would become the highest-ranked group.

prompt: Imagining one hydrogen on a prochirality center replaced by deuterium gives an R chirality center. What is that hydrogen called?

choices.text: The pro-R hydrogen
The pro-S hydrogen
choices.why: The label follows the result of replacing that atom: replacement giving R means pro-R.

choices.text: The Re hydrogen
choices.why: Re and Si name the faces of planar sp2 carbons, not atoms on tetrahedral prochirality centers.

choices.text: An R hydrogen, because the hydrogen itself is a chirality center
choices.why: A hydrogen atom has only one bond and can't be a chirality center; the label describes what its replacement does to the carbon.

explanation: Of the two identical atoms on a prochirality center, the atom whose replacement leads to an R chirality center is said to be pro-R, and the atom whose replacement leads to an S chirality center is pro-S.

prompt: A prochirality center carries two hydrogens, Ha and Hb. Imagining Ha replaced by deuterium gives an S chirality center. What is Hb?

choices.text: Pro-R
Pro-S, the same as Ha, because the two hydrogens are identical
choices.why: The hydrogens are identical as atoms, but they sit in mirror-image positions: replacing the other one gives the opposite configuration.

choices.text: Neither; only one hydrogen on a prochirality center gets a label
choices.why: Both are labeled: one is pro-R and the other pro-S.

choices.text: It can't be known without replacing Hb as well
choices.why: Replacing Hb puts deuterium where Ha's replacement left ¹H, giving the enantiomer, so its label must be the opposite one.

explanation: Replacing Ha leads to an S chirality center, so Ha is pro-S. Replacing Hb instead gives the mirror-image center, R, so Hb is pro-R. As with ethanol's −CH2OH carbon, the two hydrogens lead to the two enantiomers.

prompt: On the −CH2OH carbon of ethanol, look with hydrogen Hb pointing directly away from you. The groups OH, CH3 and the other hydrogen, Ha, run clockwise in that order. Is Ha pro-R or pro-S?

choices.text: Pro-R
Pro-S
choices.why: Replacing Ha with deuterium gives OH > CH3 > D > Hb. With Hb, now lowest, pointing away, OH → CH3 → D runs clockwise: R, so Ha is pro-R.

choices.text: Neither; Ha and Hb are identical, so they can't be told apart
choices.why: They are identical atoms, but they can be distinguished by imagining one replaced by deuterium, which gives either an R or an S center.

choices.text: It can't be decided, because Hb, not Ha, is pointing away
choices.why: That is the right view: once Ha becomes deuterium, Hb is the lowest-ranked group, which is the one that should point away.

explanation: Imagine Ha replaced by ²H. The ranking becomes OH > CH3 > ²H > ¹H (Hb), because deuterium outranks protium but stays below the other groups. With Hb, the lowest-ranked group, pointing away, OH → CH3 → ²H runs clockwise, giving an R center. The atom whose replacement leads to an R center is pro-R.

prompt: In the citric acid cycle, H2O adds to fumarate to give (S)-malate. On which face of the fumarate carbon does the −OH add?

choices.text: The Si face
The Re face
choices.why: The text states that −OH adds to the Si face. The face name doesn't have to match the product's R/S letter.

choices.text: Both faces equally
choices.why: Equal addition to both faces would give a racemic mixture. This enzyme reaction gives only (S)-malate.

choices.text: Neither; fumarate is achiral, so its carbons have no faces
choices.why: Fumarate is achiral but prochiral: its planar sp2 carbons have Re and Si faces.

explanation: A large number of biological reactions involve prochiral compounds. In the citric acid cycle, addition of −OH occurs on the Si face of a fumarate carbon and gives (S)-malate as product.

prompt: Yeast alcohol dehydrogenase catalyzes the reaction of ethanol with NAD⁺. Which describes its stereochemistry?

choices.text: Only the pro-R hydrogen is removed from ethanol, and it adds only to the Re face of NAD⁺
Only the pro-S hydrogen is removed from ethanol, and it adds only to the Si face of NAD⁺
choices.why: Deuterium-labeling studies showed the opposite: exclusive removal of the pro-R hydrogen and addition to the Re face.

choices.text: Either hydrogen is removed at random, because the two hydrogens of ethanol are identical
choices.why: The removal is exclusive to the pro-R hydrogen. The enzyme distinguishes the two hydrogens even though they look identical.

choices.text: Only the pro-R hydrogen is removed, but it adds to either face of NAD⁺
choices.why: The addition is also selective: it occurs only on the Re face of NAD⁺.

explanation: Studies with deuterium-labeled substrates have shown that the reaction of ethanol with NAD⁺, catalyzed by yeast alcohol dehydrogenase, occurs with exclusive removal of the pro-R hydrogen from ethanol and with addition only to the Re face of NAD⁺.

prompt: The conversion of citrate to cis-aconitate in the citric acid cycle occurs with loss of a pro-R hydrogen. What does this show about the mechanism?

choices.text: The OH and H groups leave from opposite sides of the molecule
The OH and H groups leave from the same side of the molecule
choices.why: Loss of the pro-R hydrogen specifically implies that the H and OH leave from opposite sides.

choices.text: Either hydrogen can be lost, so nothing about the mechanism can be learned
choices.why: Only the pro-R hydrogen is lost, and that selectivity is what reveals the mechanism.

choices.text: The reaction adds water rather than removing it
choices.why: Citrate loses water (OH and H) to form cis-aconitate.

explanation: Determining the stereochemistry of reactions at prochirality centers is a powerful method for studying detailed mechanisms in biochemical reactions. The conversion of citrate to cis-aconitate occurs with loss of a pro-R hydrogen, implying that the OH and H groups leave from opposite sides of the molecule.
